findings.text: The summary table presents seven schedule-policy choices without marking that 'priority' is not a value the policy layer accepts, and none of the seven is marked authoritative where the report's own Q3 gives six. Input: --schedule-policy priority. The installed CLI literal does offer it (server_args.py:744-759: lpm, random, fcfs, dfs-weight, lof, priority, routing-key), but neither policy enum contains it (CacheAwarePolicy lpm/dfs-weight at schedule_policy.py:204-217; CacheAgnosticPolicy fcfs/lof/random/routing-key in the same block), and the only resolver is _validate_and_adjust_policy (schedule_policy.py:307-323), which tries CacheAwarePolicy(policy), then CacheAgnosticPolicy(policy), then raises ValueError(f"Unknown schedule_policy: {policy=}"). init_schedule_policy (scheduler.py:1340-1348) passes the server_args string to SchedulePolicy unchanged, and a grep of the whole srt tree finds no other constructor or mapping. So 'priority' is a CLI choice that fails at policy init; priority ordering is instead the separate enable_priority_scheduling flag (server_args.py:760-764), which Q3 does describe. Epistemic limit: this is source-level resolution, not an executed failure — the engine was not launched to confirm, and this review did not launch it. A reader acting on the seven-choice row would pass a flag the installed code rejects; the report should either drop 'priority' from the lever set or state which list governs and why they differ.

The report states its own access as isolation accomplished -- 'No request was sent to the lane' (line 5) and 'this node did not query the live lane: its access is source inspection only' (line 262) -- while the run's own record shows an outbound request addressed at that lane. Input: the second dispatch's stream contains curl --max-time 8 --fail-with-body --silent --show-error http://98dci4-gpu-0003:18810/model_info, exit 6 'curl: (6) Could not resolve host: 98dci4-gpu-0003'. Port 18810 is the DSv4.1 profile's own port (imas_ambix/agent/profiles/deepseek-v4-1-flash.toml:536), so the command was aimed at the live lane. No request reached the engine: the failure is at DNS resolution, before any connection. The manifest does not overstate this -- its follow_ons records that a live readback of effective_max_running_requests_per_dp was attempted and failed because the hostname did not resolve -- but the report is the plan's evidence artifact and carries none of that. The first sentence is literally true; the second describes the node's access as policy rather than as a failed attempt, which is the version a reader is likelier to quote. The honest and better line is the one the manifest already has. Nothing was mutated; this is a framing defect, not a harm.

The context sentence describes the running cap as sitting above a knee the plan has already withdrawn: '36 sits above the plan's measured aggregate-throughput knee (~22)'. Input: a reader who takes that line as current. Plan section 3-landed records the opposite -- 'The profile's flat claim holds on its stated range; the ~22 knee is not present' and 'No width above 36 was ever logged, so no knee below the cap appears -- which is the profile's justification for 36'. The pre-remeasure text the line echoes is still present earlier in the same plan (sections 1 and 2 carry 'knee ~ 22' and 'peaks near 22 concurrent at about 500 tok/s'), so the sentence is faithful to an older layer of the document and stale against its own landed result. It is context rather than an answer, and it changes none of the seven answers; but section 4 is the evidence section other sections consume, and a reader could conclude the 36 cap rests on a measured knee when the plan's position is that no knee below the cap exists.
